title: The creation of the UN
subject: histoire
description: On **June 26, 1945**, **51** countries signed the Charter of the United Nations in San Francisco. Born from the ashes of the Second World War, the UN set out to spare the world the scourge of war.

hero.hook: After two world wars, one bold idea: make nations talk before they shoot.

blocks.text: On **June 26, 1945**, **51** countries signed the **Charter of the United Nations** in San Francisco. The goal was plain: to spare future generations the scourge of war. The UN was not just another alliance. It was meant to be a common framework for the whole world.
The project tried to hold together two ideas that often clash: the equality of nations, and the real weight of the victorious great powers.

sections.title: The failure of the League of Nations

blocks.text: The idea of [[global governance]], shared rules between states, goes back a long way. After 1918, American president **Woodrow Wilson** launched the **League of Nations**. Based in Geneva, it aimed to settle conflicts through law. But the American Senate, attached to [[Isolationism]], refused to join. Without the United States, the League carried little weight.

blocks.caption: The League of Nations in Geneva, the fragile ancestor of the UN

blocks.text: The League officially survived the whole of the Second World War. It was dissolved only in **1946**, so that it could hand its assets to the new UN.

With no real force and no [[Blue Helmets]], it could not stop Japan in Manchuria or Italy in Ethiopia. Its collapse taught the founders of the UN one rule: keep the great powers inside, and give the institution real leverage.

sections.title: The Security Council and the veto

blocks.text: The Charter created a body with two heads. The **General Assembly** gives every state a voice. The **Security Council** acts as the executive: sanctions, and the use of force. To keep the strongest at the table, the drafters invented the [[Veto power in the Security Council]].

blocks.caption: The Security Council chamber, the political heart of the UN

blocks.text: Five victors of 1945 became permanent members: the United States, the USSR, the United Kingdom, France, and China. Each one can block a resolution. From the start of the Cold War, the veto often froze the Council whenever a conflict touched the interests of one bloc.

sections.title: What the UN gets right out of the spotlight

blocks.text: When diplomacy stalls, the specialized agencies change lives. The **WHO**, the World Health Organization, coordinates global health and made the eradication of **smallpox** possible in 1980. **UNICEF** (children), the **UNHCR** (refugees), **UNESCO** (culture), the **FAO** (food): a technical network that reaches past borders.

Where the League had failed, the UN became essential to the running of the modern world: civil aviation, telecoms, food aid, refugees. Less dramatic than the Council, this work is its real daily success.

Today the UN has **193** members. Its 1945 structure, shaped in large part by [[The Yalta Conference (February 1945)]] between Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin, no longer matches the world. India, Brazil, and Africa are demanding a reform of the veto. The annual budget, about **3 billion** dollars, is tiny next to the ambitions.
The UN headquarters in New York is international ground: its own security, its own fire service, and even postage stamps you can use only from inside the building.

blocks.caption: Signing the Charter of the United Nations, San Francisco, 1945

blocks.text: Created in **1945** to fix the failure of the League, the UN pairs a powerful but often paralyzed Security Council with agencies whose humanitarian work changed the 20th century.
